```{=html}
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The idea in one table: a 300 MW data center joins Prairie Town (illustrative)</p><p class="lx-hint">The town's demand on two real-shape days, and with the campus's steady 240 MW added to every hour.</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table f8-fbt"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Day</th><th scope="col">Town's busiest hour</th><th scope="col">Town's quietest hour</th><th scope="col">With the campus: busiest and quietest</th><th scope="col">Campus share of the day</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>29 July 2025</td><td>450 MW</td><td>298 MW</td><td>690 MW and 538 MW</td><td>39%</td></tr><tr><td>17 April 2025</td><td>300 MW</td><td>216 MW</td><td>540 MW and 456 MW</td><td>48%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><ul><li><b>Its contract.</b> Up to 300 MW: on 29 July 2025 the busiest hour could reach 750 MW.</li><li><b>Homes.</b> 240 MW all year is 2,102,400 MWh: as much as about 195,000 average U.S. homes buy in a year (10,791 kWh each), and 85% of the town's own use.</li><li><b>The year.</b> With the campus, demand is above the town's 2025 record in 8,690 of 8,760 hours; the load factor rises from 63% to 76%.</li><li><b>Requests.</b> ERCOT counted about 474 GW of large loads asking to connect (June 2026), 5.2 times its record peak of 91,134 MW: requests are not demand.</li><li><b>The wait.</b> Built in 24 months, connected after 36: 12 idle months.</li><li><b>Cooling.</b> Evaporative cooling: uses water: some evaporates to carry heat away; less electricity for cooling. Closed-loop cooling: little water once the loop is filled; often more electricity, for fans and chillers.</li><li><b>Jobs and taxes.</b> 1,000 workers for 24 months make 2,000 job-years, then 50 permanent jobs; $1,000M of property at 1.0% pays $10.0M a year in local tax (illustrative).</li><li><b>Who pays.</b> If the utility builds wires for the campus and the company cancels, the cost can land on other customers, unless a large-load tariff makes the company pay.</li></ul><p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you work through this step by step: the day, a spring day, the homes, the year, the requests, the wait, water, jobs and taxes, and who pays.</p>
```

::: {#explain .lx-sec}

## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="f08-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>A load, not a town</dt><dd>A <span class="lx-term" data-term="large-load">large load</span> is one customer that draws as much as a town: here, a steady 240 MW against Prairie Town's busiest hour of 450 MW.</dd>
<dt>Flat, around the clock</dt><dd>It adds as much at night as at the busiest hour, so the town's quiet hours rise most in share.</dd>
<dt>Energy, not peak</dt><dd>240 MW all year equals about 195,000 average U.S. homes' yearly electricity, but that compares energy, not power in any hour.</dd>
<dt>Requests, not demand</dt><dd>ERCOT's requests to connect were 5.2 times its record peak in 2026: many are duplicates or will never be built.</dd>
<dt>Who pays</dt><dd>The utility builds first; a <span class="lx-term" data-term="large-load-tariff">large-load tariff</span> decides how much the campus pays, and how much other customers do.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>MW of computers, MW from the grid</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **[Power usage effectiveness]{.lx-term term="power-usage-effectiveness"} (PUE)** is a data center's total electricity divided by its computing equipment's electricity.
- **For example,** 200 MW of computers at a PUE of 1.2 need 200 × 1.2 = 240 MW from the grid.
- **Sizes in [MW-IT]{.lx-term term="mw-it"}** count the computers only; the grid must plan for the whole campus.
- **Cooling works harder on hot days,** so a real campus is not perfectly flat; this lesson keeps it flat to show the idea.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Requests, forecasts and ranges</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **A request is a place in line,** not a building: ERCOT's 474 GW of requests is 5.2 times its record peak of 91,134 MW.
- **A range, not a number.** Berkeley Lab's scenarios put U.S. data centers at 325 to 580 TWh in 2028, 6.7% to 12% of U.S. electricity; planners study the whole range.
- **Read next.** Why connecting takes years: Analyst lesson [A6](a06-interconnection.html). Who pays for a wait: case file [CF7](cf7-cost-of-waiting.html).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Adding a flat load to a load-duration curve</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

A flat load of $c$ MW shifts every hour up by $c$, so the [load factor]{.lx-term term="load-factor"} becomes

$$\text{LF} = \frac{\bar d + c}{d_{\max} + c} = \frac{281.9 + 240}{450 + 240} = 0.756$$

- $\bar d$ is the town's average hour of 2025 (MW) and $d_{\max}$ its busiest hour (MW); a flat load pushes LF toward 1.
- **A load that is not flat** must be added hour by hour before sorting: the busiest hours of the sum need not be the busiest hours of either part.
- **Next.** The Grid Room sandbox (SB2, upcoming) adds a large load to a regional grid; resource adequacy (A5, upcoming) asks whether supply is enough in every hour.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Whether the wires can carry the campus: voltage, lines and stability are Analyst lesson <a href="a17-physical-feasibility.html">A17</a>.</li>
<li>Which plants run for it, and at what price: the merit order is <a href="08-merit-order.html">lesson 8</a>.</li>
<li>The emissions it causes or may claim: Analyst lesson A10 (upcoming).</li>
<li>Shifting some of its work in time: flexible demand is <a href="a07-flexible-demand.html">A7</a>.</li>
<li>Real campuses' changing draw, and the real numbers for water, jobs and taxes, which differ by place.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<p class="lx-lede">Practice, about 10 minutes: three myths, then five questions.</p>
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="f08-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="night" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A data center uses its power mostly at night, so it does not raise the busiest hour.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It runs around the clock: in this lesson it adds 240 MW in every hour, so the town's busiest hour on 29 July 2025 rises from 450 to 690 MW.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="requests" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Requests to connect show how much new demand will arrive.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. ERCOT's requests were about 474 GW in June 2026, 5.2 times its record peak: some are duplicates, and many will never be built.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="jobs" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “1,000 people building a campus for two years means 1,000 permanent jobs.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. That is 2,000 <span class="lx-term" data-term="job-year">job-years</span>, which end when building ends; the campus then needs its own, smaller permanent staff.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="f08">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="homes" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A data center averages 120 MW all year. About how many average U.S. homes (10,791 kWh a year each) use as much electricity in a year?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">About 9,700</li><li data-value="b">About 97,000</li><li data-value="c">About 120,000</li><li data-value="d">About 970,000</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>About 97,000: 120 MW × 8,760 h = 1,051,200 MWh, ÷ 10.791 MWh a home = 97,415.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="spring" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">At 03:00 on 17 April 2025, Prairie Town draws 216 MW. Add the campus's 240 MW. Is the total above the town's 2025 record of 450 MW?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Yes: 456 MW</li><li data-value="b">No: 216 MW</li><li data-value="c">No: exactly 450 MW</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Yes: 216 + 240 = 456 MW, above the record, at the quietest hour of a mild day.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="ercot" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">ERCOT counted about 474 GW of large-load requests; its record peak is 91,134 MW. About how many times the peak is that?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">About 2</li><li data-value="b">About 5.2</li><li data-value="c">About 10</li><li data-value="d">About 52</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>About 5.2: 474 GW = 474,000 MW, and 474,000 ÷ 91,134 = 5.2.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="tax" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">$800M of taxable property, at a local tax rate of 1.5%, pays how much a year?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$1.2M</li><li data-value="b">$12M</li><li data-value="c">$120M</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$12M: 800 × 1.5% = 12. It is a <span class="lx-term" data-term="transfer">transfer</span> from the owner to local budgets.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="exit" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">Which term of a large-load tariff makes a customer that cancels pay toward wires built for it?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">An exit fee</li><li data-value="b">A time-of-use price</li><li data-value="c">Net metering</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>An exit fee; a minimum bill does the same while it stays connected (<a href="a04-retail-tariffs.html">A4</a>).</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<li>Souder, D. (2026). <a href="https://insidelines.pjm.com/providing-reliable-electricity-in-a-new-reality/">Providing Reliable Electricity in a New Reality</a>. PJM Inside Lines, 15 October 2026.</li>
<li>EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=97&amp;t=3">How much electricity does an American home use?</a> Frequently Asked Questions, updated 8 January 2024.</li>
<li>The town's hourly shapes: EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/">Hourly Electric Grid Monitor</a> (Form EIA-930), Southwest Power Pool, 2025 (accessed 2 November 2026).</li>
<li>Li et al. (2026). Accepted paper on the cost of delayed grid energization for large loads, 2026 North American Power Symposium (NAPS), presented October 2026; DOI pending.</li>
</ul>
</div>
```
